strengths: Novel problem formulation: Recasting discrete sequence optimization as trajectory planning in edit space provides an intuitive middle ground between opaque diffusion models and myopic LLMs, with natural support for variable-length operations.

Interpretable and executable reasoning traces: Explicit INSERT/DELETE/REPLACE trajectories provide transparent, verifiable, and user-controllable reasoning with parse-and-execute consistency checks—significant practical advantages over black-box generation.

Elegant supervision design: Levenshtein DP backtracing provides principled, deterministic minimal-edit supervision; combining process supervision (edit scripts) with outcome supervision effectively induces validity-preserving and minimal-edit biases.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Two domains (proteins and molecules), multiple well-chosen baselines, rich metrics (validity, success, uniqueness, novelty, off-target drift), informative ablations, and extensive appendices enabling reproducibility.

Strong results on variable-length edits: Impressive gains in the harder setting (89/100 vs. 42/100 success; 76/78 vs. 14/30 novelty), demonstrating clear benefits when edit space becomes combinatorial.

Honest limitations discussion: Authors clearly contextualize oracle reliability issues, model capacity dependencies, and synthetic label concerns rather than merely listing them, enhancing credibility.
Reproducibility: Code released with detailed training details, hyperparameters, and clear methodology descriptions supporting community adoption.
weaknesses: Limited protein experimental scope: Single property (GFP fluorescence), small dataset (3,280 SFT examples), fixed source anchor, and synthetic indel augmentation with pseudo-labels significantly constrain claims about protein engineering applicability.

Oracle and evaluation reliability: No experimental validation of predictions; protein oracle trained only on substitutions (not indels), making full-action results unreliable; molecular evaluation relies on proxy properties (LogP, QED) rather than real bioactivity, limiting biological significance.

Molecular results less compelling than framed: Direct SFT already achieves strong goal attainment (0.629/0.745 strict/loose); STRIDE-SFT actually decreases performance (0.579/0.684); RL gains are primarily in stability (off-target drift reduction), not objective achievement, with main benefits abstract ('structured interface').

Model capacity dependency and scalability concerns: ~80% index following for Qwen3-14B vs. <60% for Qwen3-4B raises fundamental questions about scaling to longer sequences; limited exploration of this critical trade-off and whether bottleneck is fundamental or capacity-limited.

Unclear when/why trajectories provide genuine benefit: Gains largest on variable-length (combinatorial) edits; replace-only improvements modest; unclear if benefit derives from explicit trajectories or from RL regularization; missing ablations and analysis of which patterns/landscapes/scales benefit most.

Incomplete hyperparameter justification: Molecular reward thresholds appear hand-tuned without sensitivity analysis; KL coefficient β=0.001 fixed without ablation; how thresholds were determined (grid search vs. domain expertise) not explained.
Missing computational analysis: No discussion of inference latency or computational cost relative to baselines; edit trajectory generation likely adds overhead important for practical deployment.
Statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars despite reasonable sample sizes (N=100 proteins, 500×14 molecules); all comparisons reported as point estimates.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation combining strengths of trajectory planning with LLM-based generation; addresses real limitations of both diffusion models and vanilla LLMs
Sound technical approach with Levenshtein-based trajectory generation, parse-execute consistency checks, and principled reward alignment using KL regularization
Strong empirical results on protein benchmarks: 42%→89% success on GFP full-action edits; novelty improvements particularly striking (14/30→76/78); generalization to AAV demonstrated
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple benchmarks, thoughtful ablations (Table 4a showing structured edit value), specialist baselines, and cross-backbone analysis (Table 14)

Honest and thorough limitations discussion: acknowledges GFP as oracle stress-test, documents execution degradation (95% at 1-3 vs 26% at 3-10 mutations), discusses model-capacity requirements, includes impact statement on dual-use concerns
Detailed reproducibility support: hyperparameters in Appendix C, datasets clearly identified, evaluation metrics well-defined, multiple implementation details provided
Closed-loop iterative refinement shows consistent novelty gains (84.3%→97.0%) under fixed budget, demonstrating practical inference-time control
Attribution study (Table 4a) isolates trajectory contribution from verbosity, showing 23→40 novelty gain from structured edits alone
weaknesses: Severe long-horizon execution limitation: only 26/100 success at 3-10 mutations vs 95/100 at 1-3 mutations; fundamentally constrains practical applicability beyond short edit budgets

Strong model-capacity and architecture dependency: Qwen3-14B achieves ~80% index accuracy while Qwen3-4B drops below 60%; Phi-4 completely fails (32 vs 61 success, Table 14); requires customizable reasoning regions limiting reproducibility

Mixed results on molecular optimization: STRIDE-SFT actually *worsens* controllability vs vanilla SFT (Shift Rate 0.948→0.983); only RL post-training recovers benefits, suggesting structured trajectory interface alone is not beneficial and may complicate generation
All results are in-silico with no wet-lab validation; GFP oracle trained on substitutions only, making full-action results speculative; acknowledged need for validation before practical use

GRPO training instability documented: mode collapse produces 'success ∼100/100 with unique improvements only ∼2/100'; authors acknowledge success metric alone can be 'vacuously satisfied by degenerate policy', requiring careful metric reporting
Code availability unclear: abstract references 'code:' with blank URL; no code provided in submission despite comprehensive hyperparameter details
Synthetic indel augmentation introduces unanalyzed bias: pseudo-labels from pre-trained fluorescence predictor triple training data (3,280→10,442) without label-quality analysis
Incomplete ablations of reward design complexity: molecular reward has multiple terms (Ivalid, Rprop, Rsim, Rstable) but component contributions not systematically ablated in main paper

Statistical rigor: results appear to be single runs without confidence intervals or significance tests (note in E.5: 'single-run external LLM sampler'); cross-validation or multiple seeds not reported
Per-task molecular results scattered across paper and appendix; shift metrics show inconsistent improvements (e.g., 'Less soluble + more HBD' shifts worsen with GSPO: 2.841→2.893)
